seo.title: Karmic tail 3 10 7 compatibility: a house on wheels
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 10 7 compatibility: The Empress, The Wheel of Fortune and The Chariot. Why this couple's home keeps moving, and who holds the reins.

title: The 3-10-7 karmic tail in compatibility: a house, a wheel and a wagon
short: In a compatibility matrix the three numbers of the 3-10-7 tail add up on their own: 3 + 7 = 10. The Empress is the house, The Chariot is the wagon, and together they make The Wheel of Fortune. This is the tail of a couple whose home is always on the road: the shared wish is a nest of their own and a full larder, the path runs through rounds of good and bad luck, and the main task is to decide together where to go and who holds the reins.

sections.h2: The first clue: the middle is the sum of the ends
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail is not calculated from the two outer numbers. Each point of the couple is counted on its own: add the matching points of the two personal matrices and reduce the sum to 22 or less. The couple's middle is the sum of the two personal middles, not the entry plus the main task. So the coincidence in 3-10-7 is a property of these particular numbers, not a rule of the calculation: The Empress plus The Chariot equal The Wheel exactly, with no reduction needed.

The site's engine shows where it comes from. In 92.5% of couples with this tail, the partners' personal tails are 21-7-13 and 9-3-21. The first has The Chariot in the middle of their personal tail, the second has The Empress. In the couple's matrix these two cards move out to the edges: The Empress becomes the entry, The Chariot the main task. And the couple's middle is made of the two of them: 7 + 3 = 10. One partner's wagon and the other's house, added together, make a wheel.

In the remaining 7.5% of couples the partners' tails are 21-10-16 and 9-18-9. There the couple's Wheel is the middle of one partner's own personal tail, with the other partner's Moon added to it: 10 + 18 = 28, and 2 + 8 = 10. The entry, though, is built the same way for every couple with this tail: one partner's World and the other's Hermit, 21 + 9 = 30, which reduces to 3. The wide world and a lonely light in a cabin together make The Empress — a house in the middle of open country.

The tail is rare: it turns up in roughly one couple in 1,171 (0.085%), 84th of the 97 couple tails. As a personal tail, 3-10-7 does not exist at all. In a personal matrix the entry M is the main task D plus the centre of the chart, and with a 7 as the main task no centre can produce a 3 at the entry. So no one brings this triple with them: it only appears in a couple.
History has a well-known name for a house set on wheels: the settlers' covered wagon. And one such family lived the 3-10-7 tail in such detail that their daughter wrote it all down, scene by scene.

sections.h2: Little House: the family that carried its home in a wagon
paragraphs: Laura Ingalls Wilder wrote a series of books about her family: eight came out between 1932 and 1943, and a ninth was published after her death, in 1971. In them Ma and Pa — Caroline and Charles Ingalls — travel from the Big Woods of Wisconsin to Kansas, back to Wisconsin, to Plum Creek in Minnesota and on to Silver Lake in Dakota. Bows go up on the wagon, the canvas is stretched over them, beds are made underneath. Almost every time they arrive, Pa builds a house, and almost every time the house is left behind.
Wilder is quoted here in her own words, from the original American editions.

In the books it is Pa who wants the road and Ma who guards the home. In a couple with the 3-10-7 tail the roles are not split by gender, and Wilder herself shows it. When Laura, still a girl, begs to go on West, Pa tells her: "You and I want to fly like the birds." The wandering foot passed to the daughter, and in the next generation she is the one who takes the reins.

sections.h2: Entry — The Empress: the shepherdess comes out only at home
paragraphs: In the Big Woods Pa carves a Christmas bracket for Ma: a carved back, a little vine around the edge, a star at the top. Ma stands her china woman on it — a shepherdess with a china bonnet and little gilt china shoes. From that moment the family has a sign of home, and it is made by two pairs of hands: the shelf is his, the figure is hers.

The shepherdess travels half a continent with them and never breaks. In Kansas Pa lays a floor of oak puncheons, Ma sets the figure on the mantel-shelf and says: "There. Now we're living like civilized folks again." At Silver Lake the family lives in a makeshift shanty at the railroad camp, and Pa asks: "But where's the china shepherdess, Caroline?" Ma answers: "I haven't unpacked the shepherdess, Charles. We aren't living here, we're only staying till you get our homestead." It comes out only on their own claim, when Pa says, "We're settled at last on our homestead claim," and drives the nail for the bracket himself.

This is **the couple's common language** — point M, the entry to the task. Both need a home where the shepherdess stands on the shelf rather than lying in a box. The Empress in this tail is not the card of one "home-loving" partner. It is a wish the couple shares completely.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. Look at Ma and Pa arguing when Pa is offered work in Dakota. Pa: "We can get a hundred and sixty acres out west, just by living on it, and the land's as good as this is, or better." Ma: "But we're settled here. We've got the farm." Both are speaking the language of The Empress — land, plenty, a place of their own. The only difference is where that place lies: for one it is already here, for the other a little further on, where there is more. The argument of a couple with this tail is rarely house against road. More often it is two houses against each other: the one they have and the one they might have.

Benebell Wen has a word that gives away this Empress's secret. She writes that The Empress "can harness the laws of nature in her favor". Harness is a driver's word. The mistress of the garden is a driver too: she harnesses rain, sun and season. So in a couple with this tail the question "who is driving?" comes up already at the entry — it is just still about the vegetable beds, not the road.

In a couple today this looks familiar. Two people rent a flat, and one of them never unpacks the boxes: "We're only here for now." Two people renovate and argue not about tiles but about whether to put money into walls they will leave anyway. Two people talk about a house of their own for years and cannot agree which town it is in.

sections.h2: Middle — The Wheel of Fortune: a bet with Uncle Sam
paragraphs: The middle of the tail is how the couple lives the way from the wish to the task. Waite calls The Wheel "the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe" and "the flux of human life". For Ma and Pa that flux can be read in a single field.

On Plum Creek Pa sows wheat and, when it is barely up, brings home a wagon piled high with lumber. "Here's your new house, Caroline!" — "But the wheat's hardly up yet!" — "That's all right. They let me have the lumber, and we'll pay for it when we sell the wheat." A house of sawed lumber, with glass windows, built on the strength of a harvest. When the heads are already heavy, Pa lists what will come after the harvest: out of debt, a buggy for him, a silk dress for Ma. All three cards are already in that dream: plenty, the luck of the harvest, and a carriage. Then at Saturday dinner Pa says he has never seen such a crop: they are rich now and can have anything they want. Laura looks through the open door, and the sunshine dims. It is a cloud of grasshoppers. The Wheel turns at the very moment the couple reaches its top.

What follows is the reason to read this chapter. Pa says: "Don't worry, Caroline. We did all we could, and we'll pull through somehow." Ma slips a pillow under his head while he sleeps on the floor. No one blames anyone for the lumber. Soon Pa sets out on foot to the east, where the grasshoppers did not reach, to hire out for other men's harvest, and walks two hundred miles. A man who all his life has pulled west goes east, because the home needs it. The night before, he plays "Oh, Susanna" on his fiddle: "I'm going to California."

Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the site follows for couples, describes The Wheel in a couple through two poles. In the minus, the couple blames fate and each other, lives on a swing between silence and quarrel, and finds it hard to be together while something still holds them. In the plus, a partner is accepted in any state, and change becomes a reason to move. The Wheel does not ask permission. The couple decides only one thing: whether each turn of it becomes a charge against the other.

The Wheel had already turned earlier, when they left Kansas. That day the family eats for dinner the seed potatoes they had been saving for planting, and Pa says: "There's no great loss without some small gain." The store for next year's crop becomes a meal for the road. This is how The Wheel treats The Empress: what was saved for later has to be eaten now.

And at Silver Lake Pa states the law of The Wheel outright. To get a claim, the law says you must live on it for five years, and Pa tells his daughters: "I've bet Uncle Sam fourteen dollars against a hundred and sixty acres of land, that we can make out to live on the claim for five years." Ma answers: "I don't like to think of it as gambling." Pa: "Everything's more or less a gamble, Caroline." One couple, two views of The Wheel: for him life is a bet, for her an order with no room for chance. Waite, as it happens, is on Ma's side: behind the symbol of The Wheel he sees "the denial of chance". But both are right, and it helps a couple with this tail to know which of the two sees the bet and which sees the order.

The most exact image of the middle is in The Long Winter. Blizzard after blizzard cuts the little town off from the trains, and the family grinds wheat in a hand coffee mill to bake bread. "The coffee mill's handle ground round and round, it must not stop." A small wheel inside the kitchen holds the house together while the big wheel of winter turns outside. Pa says: "It can't beat us! It's got to quit sometime and we don't." A couple with this tail today has its own coffee mill too: the work nobody notices and without which no crisis can be got through.

sections.h2: Main task — The Chariot: who holds the reins
paragraphs: The main task of the tail is read above all through what the couple fails at. With Ma and Pa it is visible from the first pages of Little House on the Prairie. Pa says: "Seeing you don't object, I've decided to go see the West." Ma only answers: "Oh, Charles, must we go now?" One decided, the other kept quiet. The reins are in one pair of hands, and silence counts as consent.

A year later word comes that soldiers will move the settlers out of Indian Territory: the family, as Pa himself admits, has settled three miles over the line, on Osage land. Ma asks: "What is the matter, Charles? Where are we going?" Pa answers: "Durned if I know! But we're going." This is a Chariot without a direction. Wen writes of the reversed Chariot that the Seeker **must reconsider direction** and make sure the movement is going the right way. The wagon has power, but no aim.

Lisovskaya sets out The Chariot among a couple's tasks very concretely: to dare a move together, not to compete for the lead, to balance work and the relationship, not to demand that a partner give up their own goals for someone else's. She also writes that couples with The Chariot often move house in search of a home of their own. It could have been written about the Ingalls family.

Yet Ma and Pa did have an agreement, and in the end it stopped the wagon. Pa tells Laura: "Your Ma was a school-teacher when we met, and when she came West with me I promised that our girls would have a chance to get book learning. That's why we stopped here, so close to a town that has a school." Ma agreed to the road on a condition. A few years later Laura begs to go further, and Pa answers: "You and I want to fly like the birds. But long ago I promised your Ma that you girls should go to school. You can't go to school and go West."

The last lines of that scene are the main task of the tail. Pa says: "Just so you're content, Caroline, I'm satisfied." Wilder adds: "That was true, but he did want to go West." The agreement is kept, and the wish remains. Years later Pa again gazes west from the doorway, and Ma says she was so tired of being dragged from pillar to post. He answers: "Well, I guess we are, Caroline. Don't fret. It's just that my wandering foot gets to itching, I guess."

The Chariot of this tail is not solved by one of them giving in. If the reins simply pass from one to the other, someone is still riding where they did not want to go. The road Pa gave up lived on in his fiddle: he played songs about California in a house that was not going anywhere any more. In a couple with this tail each needs a fiddle of their own — their own work, their own path — so that the shared home does not become someone's cage.

Wen gives The Chariot two observations that fit this story. First, The Chariot is **"travel not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition"**. Pa never travelled for the sake of the road; he went after land and game, that is, after The Empress. The driver in this tail carries the house rather than running from it. Second, according to Wen, the chariot bears a badge of "the union of the external sphere of rulership by man and the internal sphere of rulership by woman". In a couple with the 3-10-7 tail these spheres are not tied to gender, but the core remains: one wagon has both the world outside and the order inside in harness.

There is a small coincidence too. When Pa's sister brings him the offer of work in Dakota, Ma says: "It does seem providential, fifty dollars a month." Waite's list of meanings for The Chariot begins with the words "Succour, providence".

sections.h2: The next generation: the reins in two pairs of hands
paragraphs: Laura grew up with her father's wandering foot. At fifteen she teaches school twelve miles from home, and every Friday Almanzo Wilder comes for her in a sleigh. Once he sets out when it is forty below zero. Laura hesitates for a long time, then tells him straight: "I am going with you only because I want to get home. When I am home to stay, I will not go with you any more." The relationship begins with an honest talk about the sleigh: who is carrying whom, and why.

Later Almanzo has a young horse, Barnum, who rears as he starts. Laura asks: "Let me drive him; I would like to see if I could." Almanzo seems doubtful but gives her the lines: "Keep a tight rein on him." She drives the length of the little town, her arms tire, and she hands the lines back, warning him that she will want to drive again. Almanzo answers: "You may drive all you want to. It gives my arms a rest, too." The next time Laura says: "I do believe Barnum knows I'm driving." Almanzo takes the lines and notes: "He leans on the bit, with me." The same horse pulls differently in different hands. It is the best description of this tail's Chariot one could find: the reins pass from hand to hand, and the wagon grows lighter for it.

Before the wedding Laura asks about the reins directly: "Do you want me to promise to obey you?" Almanzo answers: "Of course not. I know it is in the wedding ceremony, but it is only something that women say. I never knew one that did it, nor any decent man that wanted her to." Laura explains why it matters to her: "I can not make a promise that I will not keep, and, Almanzo, even if I tried, I do not think I could obey anybody against my better judgment." — "I'd never expect you to." The minister marries them without the word "obey". The couple agreed on the reins before they set off.

In the posthumous book The First Four Years Laura admits she did not want to marry a farmer: a farm is too hard a place for a woman. Almanzo proposes a deal: try farming for three years, and if it does not work, turn to something else. The term is later extended. Hail flattens the wheat just before harvest, later hot dry winds ruin the crop again, the debts grow. The Wheel turns just as it did for her parents.

But near the end of the book a single long sentence shows that this couple's Chariot has found a different direction: "The incurable optimism of the farmer who throws his seed on the ground every spring, betting it and his time against the elements, seemed inextricably to blend with the creed of her pioneer forefathers that 'it is better farther on' — only instead of farther on in space, it was farther on in time, over the horizon of the years ahead instead of the far horizon of the west."

The whole tail is in that sentence, in order. Seed in the ground — The Empress. A bet against the elements — The Wheel. "Better farther on" — The Chariot. And the main discovery: The Chariot changed its axis. The father looked for something better beyond the next hill, the daughter in the next year. A wagon does not have to travel across a map to move forward.

And yet The Chariot did travel. In 1894 the Wilders loaded a covered wagon and left Dakota for Missouri, for Rocky Ridge Farm. That is where Laura wrote her books, and today it is a museum that keeps Pa's fiddle. The road the father gave up ended in the house where it was written down.

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen saw: unlike beasts in one harness
paragraphs: This section is about the cards of the Waite–Smith deck as Waite and Wen describe them; the cards on the site are drawn in their own way.

In Waite's account The Chariot is drawn by two sphinxes: the driver "has thus replied to the sphinx", and that is why they are in harness. In the historical part of his book he recalls that "in the eighteenth century white horses were yoked to the car", and that other animals have drawn the triumphal chariot too — "for example, a lion and a leopard". Two pull The Chariot, and they need not be alike: sphinxes, horses, a lion with a leopard. One driver holds them. For a couple with this tail they are two wishes in one harness: the house and the road, "here" and "farther on".

Wen points out a detail that links the two ends of the tail. The Empress is "crowned with a laurel wreath and stars", and the wreath, Wen says, "denotes victory". The charioteer, too, "wears the laurel wreaths of victory", and the curtains of his chariot are printed with stars. The house and the road wear the same insignia: there is victory both in holding your ground and in getting there.

The centre of the matrix for most couples with this tail is Temperance, and Waite writes of its angel: **"It has one foot upon the earth and one upon waters."** That is the stance of a couple living between the firm ground of the house and the moving water of the road.

And one coincidence that is hard to miss. In Waite's reversed meanings for Temperance stand "competing interests" and even "the priest who will marry the Querent". Laura and Almanzo had competing interests — the farm or the town — and a minister who would not use the word "obey" himself. It is only a coincidence, but very much in the spirit of the tail.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: what holds the house and the wagon together
paragraphs: In 92.5% of couples with this tail the centre of the matrix — the atmosphere inside the couple — is Temperance, 14. It is made of the personal centres: the partner with the 21-7-13 tail always has a centre of 8, the partner with 9-3-21 always has 6. Waite lists Temperance as "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation", and describes its main work like this: under its rule "we know in our rational part something of whence we came and whither we are going". This couple's atmosphere gives it a compass — whence and whither. Leave the compass unused, and The Chariot drives at random.

Lisovskaya sums up the minus of Temperance in one line: one partner always gives way, and the other does not notice. That is "seeing you don't object". In the plus, Temperance in a couple settles arguments by talk and compromise, keeps a balance between motion and rest, and gives a sense that things are going to plan. For the 3-10-7 tail this is a direct answer to the main task: talk about direction out loud while the wagon is still standing.

In 7.5% of couples the centre is The Hierophant, 5. Then rules and traditions set the atmosphere, and the couple's agreement resembles Pa's promise: "the girls will go to school". Among Lisovskaya's tasks for the 5 are interference from relatives and attempts to remake each other. For a tail with a wagon in it, this means that it may be a whole family, not just two people, arguing over the direction.

The couple's values — the spiritual purpose — are The Lovers in 63.7% of couples with this tail and The Devil in 36.3%. The Lovers is a choice: Ma once chose to go West, and the strength of their union rests on the choice having been hers. Waite's list for The Lovers includes "trials overcome". The Devil is what binds: lumber on credit against a harvest, a claim the law says you must live on for five years. Lisovskaya closes her chapter on The Devil with the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. For a couple with a wagon this matters: commitments can be taken on together, but neither of the two becomes the other's baggage.

sections.h2: How a couple recognises itself in the 3-10-7 tail
paragraphs: This tail is recognised by scenes, not descriptions.

ul: **Boxes in the hallway.** One partner settled in long ago, the other lives "for now". A shepherdess in a box is not a whim: for one of the two, home has not been found yet.
**"Seeing you don't object."** One partner decides about a move, a job or a big purchase, and the other stays quiet. A year later it turns out the silence was not consent but fatigue.
**Lumber against the harvest.** The couple builds, buys, moves on credit against future income. When the harvest fails, the real question is not money but who will blame whom.
**A fiddle by the door.** One gave way and stayed, but their road did not vanish. It sounds in talk of "if only we had", in other people's photos, in longing for another town.

paragraphs: What changes the script can be seen in the books too:

ul: ask "where to?" before "we're going", not after;
agree on a date to review the decision, as Laura and Almanzo did with their three years;
unpack the shepherdess where you live now, even if it is for a while;
take turns with the reins, and notice that the horse goes differently under the other hand;
leave each a fiddle of their own — work in which one can travel further without moving the shared home;
argue with each other about decisions, but not about the wheel: grasshoppers are no grounds for a reckoning.

paragraphs: The strong version of this tail is a couple that carries its home and does not lose it on the way. It has a shared "place of our own", it lives through the turns of the wheel without keeping score, and it knows where it is going and who is driving right now. Its "farther on" does not have to lie beyond the horizon. Sometimes it is the next year on the same land.
A couple's tail is counted from three points. Each is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22 or less if the sum is larger.

The person born on 07.01.1976 has the personal tail 21-7-13: entry 21, middle 7, main task 13, centre of the chart 8. The person born on 02.01.1980 has the personal tail 9-3-21: entry 9, middle 3, main task 21, centre of the chart 6.

The couple's centre: 8 + 6 = 14, Temperance. The couple's values for these dates are 6, The Lovers. This is the most common variant: personal tails 21-7-13 and 9-3-21, The Chariot in the middle for one partner and The Empress in the middle for the other.

ul: **M = 3, The Empress — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is "a place of our own": a house, land, plenty that keeps growing. Both want the same thing, but each may picture that place somewhere else.

**N = 10, The Wheel of Fortune — middle of the task.** The path goes in circles: harvest and crop failure, debt against future income, moves. The couple gets through it when they stop blaming the wheel and each other.
**D = 7, The Chariot — main task.** Choosing a direction together. Not "seeing you don't object, I've decided", but an agreement on where the house is going, and reins that pass from hand to hand.

intro: The tail does not predict moves or ruin. It shows what this couple's main conversation will be about. No one has written that conversation down in more detail than Laura Ingalls Wilder in her Little House books, the ones the TV series was later based on. Her parents carried their home in a wagon for more than ten years, and Laura and her husband faced the same task again — and solved it differently.

faq.q: What does 3-10-7 mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In a compatibility matrix, 3-10-7 is a couple's karmic tail: The Empress at the entry, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Chariot as the main task. The couple wants a shared home and plenty, goes through turns of luck, and learns to choose a direction together and share the reins.

faq.q: Can 3-10-7 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: As a karmic tail in a personal matrix, 3-10-7 never occurs: with a 7 as the main task, no centre can give a 3 at the entry. But the same numbers in the same order do appear on other lines of a personal chart. Most often it is the talent line — for people born in March with a centre of 4 or 22. Less often it is the relationship line. There the numbers have other roles, and they cannot be read as a couple's tail.

Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail the couple's karmic programme. So a search for "programme 3 10 7" in compatibility is about the same thing: the task a couple goes through together. It is the programme of a union, not of one person.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 3, 10 and 7 a couple can only get the 3-10-7 tail: the order "entry — middle — main task" is the only one here.

faq.q: Which partner is The Empress and which is The Chariot?
faq.a: All three cards belong to the couple as a whole, not to one partner, and gender has nothing to do with it. But in 92.5% of such couples one partner has The Chariot in the middle of their personal tail and the other has The Empress. So often one is closer to the road and the other to the house, and it is in the couple that these wishes add up to a shared wheel.

faq.q: Is the 3-10-7 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict ruin, moves or break-ups. It shows the couple's main conversation — about home, about turns of luck and about direction. A couple that has this conversation out loud and hands each other the reins gets its strength from this tail: the ability to carry its home and not lose it on the way.

report: In this family the china shepherdess was unpacked only once they were sure they had come home. For more than ten years Ma and Pa Ingalls carried their home in a covered wagon, and their daughter, Laura Ingalls Wilder, wrote the journey down in her Little House books. Read alongside those books, the 3-10-7 tail unfolds almost scene by scene.

The three cards of the tail add up on their own: The Empress is the house, The Chariot is the wagon, and 3 + 7 = 10, The Wheel of Fortune. This is not a rule of the calculation but a property of these particular numbers. A house set on wheels is exactly what a settlers' covered wagon is.

A couple with this tail shares one wish: a nest of their own and a full larder. The way to the main task runs through rounds of good and bad luck. And the task itself is to decide together where the house is going and who holds the reins.

report.h3: Reins in one pair of hands

report: The main task is read through what goes wrong. At the start of the road Pa says: "Seeing you don't object, I've decided to go see the West." One decided, the other kept quiet. report: Near the end of The First Four Years there is a sentence that holds the whole tail in order. The farmer throws his seed on the ground every spring, "betting it and his time against the elements", and the pioneer creed that "it is better farther on" now means **"instead of farther on in space, it was farther on in time"**. Seed is The Empress, the bet is The Wheel, "farther on" is The Chariot. The father looked for something better beyond the next hill, the daughter in the next year.

What changes the script: ask "where to?" before "we're going"; agree on a date to review the decision, as Laura and Almanzo did with their three years on the farm; unpack the shepherdess where they live now; take turns with the reins; argue about decisions, but not about the wheel.

The strong version of this tail is **a couple that carries its home and does not lose it on the way**. It has a shared "place of our own", it lives through the turns of the wheel without keeping score, and it knows where it is going and who is driving right now. Sometimes its "farther on" is the next year on the same land.
